title: chamber-m1-replace-2026-08-13
claims: This planning session diagnosed and wrote the fix for a long-running UI defect in the Ecgberht steward chamber: the newly designed M1 chamber was painting correctly on every open and then deleting itself. The investigation traced it to `ecgSealMountInline`, which paints the M1 slice, hydrates the older v0 chamber, and then calls `_ecgSealDropSlice()` — removing M1 from the document on all three branches (chamber success, stand-up, and the error path). What John had actually been looking at all along was the pre-campaign v0 dialogue, which is exactly the surface the twelve-wave chamber campaign had been trying to replace. The session also established why every automated gate stayed green through it: the existing first-paint test aborts the chamber hydrate route, so the deletion never happened under test.

The bulk of the session was spent correcting the plan's own scope, twice. Revisions 1 and 2 both treated v0 as the specification and produced a parity map that would have dragged v0's design into M1 one affordance at a time, and they assumed M1 still needed building when a live-tree check showed it was already built and wired (close, session open, the STATUS and REFINE overlays, the deliverable action, and the pulse poll all worked). John ruled the scope back to M1 exactly as drawn: the drawn mockup is the specification, v0 affordances have no claim to survive, and no v0 rescue is permitted — including retiring v0's growing-textarea say box and the test that asserts it. That ruling produced revision 3, the plan that was actually handed off.

The resulting plan is deliberately small — two waves rather than the parity campaign. Wave 1 stops the deletion at all three call sites and wires the one genuinely missing affordance, the drawn "Talk to Jarvis" say box, by emitting `data-say-input`/`data-say-send` attributes server-side (attributes only, so the C9 hash pin on the markup still holds) and handling them in the slice's existing shadow-root delegation against the current `/api/ecgberht/converse` endpoint. It also requires a non-skippable Playwright survival test that opens the Seal, lets hydration finish, and asserts M1 is still in the document, plus a CI rule banning paint tests that abort the hydrate route — the loophole that hid the bug. Wave 2 deletes v0 outright in both the Anchor and Ecgberht trees, rewrites the sibling canaries that pinned v0 symbols, and adds a by-name, by-tree guard against its return, while keeping `/api/ecgberht/chamber` alive as a data API since `speak`/`converse`/`commission_*` compile against that view model.

Two things the session was explicit about are worth carrying forward. The plan establishes a new standing law — when code is replaced, the replaced code is deleted, because a superseded surface does not sit inert, it competes, and here it won. And it ends not with a test result but with a human-eyes gate: John opens the steward himself and confirms it changed, on the grounds that every automated instrument was green for twelve waves while the surface was being deleted on every open, and the only thing that ever caught it was him looking.

This planning session produced a single Foreman-ready implementation plan, **"Make M1 survive, wire talk, delete v0"** — and most of the session's value was in getting the scope right, since the plan reached revision 3 only after two earlier attempts were thrown out. Revisions 1 and 2 had treated the old v0 chamber as the specification and assumed the new M1 chamber still needed building; both premises were wrong. Verification against the live tree showed M1 was already built and wired (shadow-root delegation already handled the × close, session opening, the STATUS and REFINE overlays, and the deliverable link; the pulse poll already drove the status table and live-status line). The plan was rewritten around the corrected premise John supplied: M1's drawn design is the spec, v0 is not a requirements document, and the goal is not "M1 renders" but "M1 survives and v0 no longer exists."

With that framing, the session narrowed the actual defect to three concrete, evidence-backed items rather than a broad parity map: `ecgSealMountInline` paints M1 and then hydrates v0 and calls `_ecgSealDropSlice()`, deleting M1 from the document on all three branches; the drawn "Talk to Jarvis…" say box carries no `data-*` hook, making it the one unwired affordance in M1; and v0 is still present in the tree. Empty/unbuilt projects were explicitly ruled out as work, since `seal_open` already serves a drawn degraded-rail face for them.

The resulting plan is two waves plus a human gate. Wave 1 stops the delete at all three call sites and wires the say box (attributes only, so the hash-pinned C9 markup signature still holds), routing it to the existing converse endpoint and painting replies in mockup classes inside the shadow root — including a requirement that the E1 refusal be *visibly* asserted, not merely engine-green. It also folds in the collateral test fallout up front: the v0 Playwright suite and a sibling Ecgberht stand-up canary that both break the moment v0 stops mounting, each to be retargeted onto M1 or recorded on the test-debt register. Wave 2 deletes the v0 renderer, its helpers and CSS in both trees, rewrites the Ecgberht pins, and adds a name-and-tree grep guard — while keeping the chamber route alive as a data API, since converse and the commission paths compile against that view-model. The plan is careful to note the grep guard is not the real instrument; Wave 1's non-skipping survival test is.

Two durable decisions came out of the session. First, the standing law it exists to establish: when code is replaced, the replaced code is deleted — a superseded surface left in the tree competes with its successor, and here it won for twelve waves. Second, an explicit human-eyes gate after Wave 2, on the honest observation that every automated gate — signed mockup, hash-pinned DOM diff, cross-family adversarial review — stayed green the entire time the surface was being deleted on every open, and the only thing that ever caught it was John looking.
